findings.title: API Misconfiguration: Enumerated Parameter Value Restriction Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Validate every parameter server-side against its declared allowed value set and reject unknown values with HTTP 400; never rely on client-side or specification-only enforcement.
findings.description: An API parameter that declares a fixed set of allowed (enumerated) values accepted a value outside that set instead of rejecting it, indicating that server-side validation of the parameter is missing or relies solely on the client/specification.
findings.impact: Missing enforcement of declared value constraints lets an attacker submit unexpected values that the application's business logic never anticipated, which can drive it into unhandled states, bypass workflow restrictions, or reach code paths intended only for specific enumerated options. On its own the impact is usually low, but it is a reliable building block for more serious logic and access-control abuse.

findings.title: Input Validation: Numeric Parameter Boundary Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce declared minimum/maximum (and length) constraints on numeric parameters server-side and reject out-of-range values.
findings.description: A numeric API parameter that declares minimum/maximum bounds accepted a value far outside the declared range instead of rejecting it, indicating missing server-side range validation.
findings.impact: Unbounded numeric input can cause integer overflow, excessive resource allocation (e.g. huge page sizes or quantities), pricing/quantity manipulation in business flows, or denial of service. The acceptance itself is low severity but frequently underpins resource-exhaustion and business-logic attacks.

findings.title: Input Validation: Parameter Type Confusion Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce strict type validation on every input: reject values whose JSON type does not match the declared schema type, and use schema validators (e.g. JSON Schema / Pydantic) at the API boundary.
findings.description: A parameter declared as a scalar type (string/number/boolean) accepted a structurally different JSON type (an array or object) without rejection, indicating the API does not enforce the JSON type of its inputs.
findings.impact: Type confusion lets an attacker substitute arrays or objects where scalars are expected, which is a primary vector for NoSQL operator injection (e.g. {"$ne": null}), authentication bypass via type juggling, and application logic errors that can corrupt data or escalate privileges depending on how the value is consumed downstream.

findings.title: Injection: HTTP Parameter Pollution
findings.remediation_brief: Define deterministic handling for duplicate parameters at every layer; reject or canonicalise repeated keys and perform validation only after canonicalisation.
findings.description: The API accepted duplicate occurrences of the same query parameter and the response differed from the single-value baseline, indicating ambiguous or inconsistent handling of repeated parameters across the application stack.
findings.impact: Inconsistent duplicate-parameter handling between front-end proxies/WAFs and the backend lets an attacker smuggle a second value past input filtering or access-control checks (e.g. one component validates the first occurrence while another uses the last), enabling filter/WAF bypass, authorization confusion, and tainted input reaching sensitive sinks.

findings.title: Misconfigured Security Header: Content-Type Confusion — Alternate Body Format Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce the expected Content-Type for each endpoint and reject requests whose body media type does not match the declared one.
findings.description: An endpoint documented to consume JSON also accepted a request body in an alternate format (form-urlencoded), showing that the server does not enforce the declared request media type.
findings.impact: Accepting multiple body formats creates a parser-differential surface: validation, authentication, or WAF rules that only inspect the expected format can be bypassed by submitting an equivalent request in another format, and form-encoded acceptance can re-enable CSRF against otherwise JSON-only (CSRF-immune) endpoints.

findings.title: Input Validation: Unbounded Resource Consumption via Pagination Parameter
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a server-side maximum page size / result-set cap that is applied regardless of the client-supplied value, and return a 400 (or clamp) when the requested size exceeds it.
findings.description: A pagination-style parameter (e.g. limit / page_size / count) accepted an extreme value and the API returned a materially larger result set, demonstrating that result-set size is not capped server-side.
findings.impact: Uncapped result sizes let an attacker force the API to assemble and serialise very large responses, exhausting database, memory, CPU and bandwidth resources and degrading or denying service for other users at low attacker cost; it also amplifies data-exfiltration when combined with broken object-level authorization.

findings.title: WebSocket: Insecure WebSocket Transport (Unencrypted ws://)
findings.remediation_brief: Serve all WebSocket endpoints over wss:// (TLS) and redirect/deny ws:// connections.
findings.description: A WebSocket endpoint is served over unencrypted ws:// rather than wss://, so all frames are transmitted in cleartext.
findings.impact: An attacker on the network path can read and tamper with WebSocket messages, including authentication tokens and session data carried on the socket, enabling session hijacking and message injection.

findings.title: WebSocket: WebSocket Handshake Accepts Arbitrary Origin (CSWSH Risk)
findings.remediation_brief: Validate the Origin header against a strict allowlist during the handshake and require a session-bound authentication token rather than relying on ambient cookies.
findings.description: The WebSocket handshake completed with an attacker-controlled Origin header and without credentials, indicating the server does not validate the Origin during the upgrade.
findings.impact: If the socket is authenticated via cookies, a malicious web page can open an authenticated WebSocket to the target on the victim's behalf (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking), reading and sending messages as the victim and exfiltrating data or performing privileged actions.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Server-Sent Events (SSE) Stream
findings.remediation_brief: Require authentication and per-subscriber authorization before establishing an event stream.
findings.description: A Server-Sent Events stream (text/event-stream) is accessible without authentication.
findings.impact: SSE streams commonly push user- or tenant-scoped events in real time; unauthenticated access leaks live data (notifications, records, presence) to any anonymous client and can disclose cross-tenant information.

findings.title: Web Misconfiguration: Server-Sent Events Stream Over Cleartext HTTP
findings.remediation_brief: Serve event streams over HTTPS only.
findings.description: A Server-Sent Events stream is served over cleartext http:// rather than https://.
findings.impact: Pushed events traverse the network in cleartext and can be intercepted or modified by a network attacker, exposing real-time data and enabling injection of forged events.

findings.title: gRPC: gRPC Server Reflection Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Disable gRPC server reflection in production builds; distribute service definitions only to authorized clients.
findings.description: The gRPC server has server reflection enabled and enumerates its full set of services and methods to any client.
findings.impact: Exposed reflection discloses the complete RPC API surface (services, methods, message schemas) to unauthenticated attackers, removing the need to obtain .proto files and accelerating targeted attacks against internal/unintended methods.

findings.title: gRPC: Insecure gRPC Transport (Plaintext / No TLS)
findings.remediation_brief: Require TLS for all gRPC endpoints and reject plaintext connections.
findings.description: The gRPC endpoint accepted a plaintext (non-TLS) connection.
findings.impact: RPC traffic, including credentials and sensitive payloads, is transmitted in cleartext and can be intercepted or tampered with by a network attacker, enabling credential theft and request/response manipulation.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Application Responses Identify Valid Accounts
findings.description: The login endpoint returns distinguishable responses (status codes, error messages, response bodies, or timing) for valid vs. invalid usernames. This enables an attacker to enumerate valid user accounts by observing differential responses to authentication attempts with different usernames.
findings.impact: An attacker can compile a list of valid user accounts, which can then be used for targeted brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, password spraying, or social engineering. Confirmed usernames dramatically reduce the search space for password attacks.
findings.remediation_brief: Return identical responses (status code, body, headers, timing) for valid and invalid usernames. Use generic error messages like 'Invalid credentials'. Implement rate limiting and account lockout. Use constant-time comparison functions.

findings.title: Enumeration: Timing-Based Username Enumeration
findings.description: The login endpoint shows a measurable timing difference between valid and invalid username submissions. Non-constant-time credential comparison or early-exit logic exposes a timing side-channel that can be exploited for username enumeration.
findings.impact: An attacker can enumerate valid usernames by measuring response latency, even when error messages are generic. Statistical analysis of timing data can reliably distinguish valid from invalid accounts across multiple samples.
findings.remediation_brief: Use constant-time comparison functions for credential checks. Hash all credentials before comparison regardless of user existence. Introduce artificial jitter to normalize response times.

findings.title: Input Validation: Improper Input Validation Results in Server Error
findings.description: An API endpoint returns a 500-series HTTP status code when sent malformed or unexpected input. This indicates the server does not properly validate inputs before processing, allowing unhandled exceptions to propagate to the client. The error response may expose stack traces, internal paths, or framework details.
findings.impact: Server errors caused by invalid input reveal that the application lacks input validation, potentially exposing information about internal architecture. Repeated 500 errors can also indicate denial-of-service attack vectors through malformed requests.
findings.remediation_brief: Validate all inputs before processing. Return 400/422 with a structured error response instead of allowing unhandled exceptions. Implement a global exception handler that logs details server-side and returns generic errors to clients.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in API Response
findings.description: API response headers or body contain internal hostnames (e.g., *.local, *.internal, *.corp). Internal hostnames reveal network topology, naming conventions, and infrastructure details that should not be exposed to external consumers.
findings.impact: Leaked internal hostnames enable targeted SSRF attacks, DNS rebinding, and internal service enumeration. Knowing internal naming conventions helps attackers craft more effective social engineering and spear-phishing campaigns.
findings.remediation_brief: Strip internal hostnames from response headers and error messages. Use a reverse proxy that rewrites backend identifiers. Configure application frameworks to suppress internal names in production.

findings.title: JWT: JWT Scope/Claim Manipulation Accepted
findings.description: The server accepted a JWT with modified scope, role, or permission claims without rejecting the tampered token. This indicates the server does not independently validate JWT claims against the authorization database, allowing privilege escalation through token manipulation.
findings.impact: An attacker can escalate privileges by modifying JWT claims (scope, role, permissions) to gain administrative or higher-privilege access. This bypasses authorization controls entirely, granting access to sensitive data and destructive operations.
findings.remediation_brief: Validate all JWT claims server-side against the authorization database. Never trust client-provided scope/role claims. Use signed, opaque tokens or verify claim integrity with asymmetric signatures.

findings.title: Session: Excessive API Session Timeout
findings.description: API bearer tokens remain valid after extended periods of inactivity. The tested token was still accepted by the server after the configured check interval (default: 30 minutes). Excessive session timeouts increase the window for token theft and replay attacks.
findings.impact: Long-lived sessions give attackers more time to exploit stolen credentials. If a token is captured via XSS, MITM, or log file exposure, the attacker has a wider window to access the API before the token naturally expires.
findings.remediation_brief: Set token expiration to 15-30 minutes for sensitive APIs. Use refresh token rotation for longer-lived sessions. Implement idle timeout detection server-side.

findings.title: Session: Session Tokens Remain Valid After Logout
aliases: Cookie Session Not Invalidated on Logout
findings.description: Cookie-based session tokens remain valid after calling the logout endpoint. The session cookie can be replayed against protected resources and continues to grant access, indicating the server does not invalidate the server-side session record on logout.
findings.impact: An attacker who captures a user's session cookie (via XSS, network sniffing, or shared workstation) can continue accessing the application even after the user logs out, as the session token remains valid server-side.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie

findings.remediation_brief: Invalidate server-side session records on logout. Clear session cookies and rotate session IDs. Implement session binding to prevent token reuse after logout.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Unhandled Application Exception
findings.description: An API response contains stack traces, exception class names, debug output, or SQL error messages. This typically occurs on 500-series responses but can also appear in 200 responses with JSON error payloads. The disclosure reveals internal implementation details.
findings.impact: Exception details expose framework versions, file paths, database schemas, and internal logic that attackers use to craft targeted exploits. SQL error messages specifically reveal database type and schema structure for injection attacks.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement a global exception handler that returns a generic error message to clients. Log full stack traces server-side only. Disable debug mode and detailed error pages in production.

findings.title: JWT: JWT Token Contains Personally Identifiable Information
findings.description: JWT access token payload contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as email, phone number, or address. JWTs are base64-encoded (not encrypted), so any party that intercepts or extracts the token can read PII directly.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains the JWT (from browser storage, server logs, Referer headers, or MITM) gains access to the user's personal data without needing to call any additional API endpoint. This violates data minimization principles (GDPR Art. 5).
findings.remediation_brief: Remove PII from JWT payloads. Use opaque tokens or encrypted JWTs (JWE) when personal data must travel with the token. Store user details server-side and look them up by subject claim.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Bearer Token Transmitted in URL Query Parameter
findings.description: Authentication tokens (access_token, bearer, jwt) are transmitted in URL query parameters rather than in headers or cookies.
findings.impact: Tokens in URLs leak via HTTP Referer headers to third-party sites, appear in server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and any URL-sharing mechanism. An attacker accessing any of these can hijack the user's session.
findings.remediation_brief: Transmit authentication tokens in the Authorization header or as HttpOnly cookies. Never pass tokens in URL query parameters.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: API Key in URL Query Parameter
findings.description: API keys are transmitted in URL query parameters (api_key, apiKey, client_secret, etc.) rather than in headers.
findings.impact: API keys in URLs leak via Referer headers, server access logs, proxy logs, and browser history. An attacker with a leaked API key gains the same API access level as the legitimate client.
findings.remediation_brief: Transmit API keys in a custom header (e.g. X-API-Key) or the Authorization header. Avoid URL query parameters for secrets.

findings.title: Session: Session Token Not Rotated After Authentication
findings.description: The session cookie retains the same value before and after authentication. An attacker who sets a pre-authentication session cookie can hijack the victim's authenticated session.
findings.impact: An attacker can set a known session token in the victim's browser (via XSS, subdomain cookie injection, or URL parameter) before the victim logs in. After login, the session token remains the same, giving the attacker a fully authenticated session.
findings.remediation_brief: Regenerate the session ID on every privilege-level change (login, logout, role escalation). Invalidate the old session immediately.

findings.title: Permissive Security Header: CORS Allows Null Origin
findings.description: The API reflects 'null' as an allowed CORS origin. Sandboxed iframes, data: URIs, and local files send Origin: null, allowing an attacker to craft pages that read cross-origin API responses.
findings.impact: An attacker can create a sandboxed iframe that sends Origin: null, which the server accepts. If credentials are allowed, the attacker can read authenticated API responses, extracting user data and tokens.
findings.remediation_brief: Never whitelist 'null' as an allowed origin. Use an explicit allowlist of trusted origins for CORS.

findings.title: GraphQL: GraphQL Field Name Suggestions Enabled
findings.description: The GraphQL server returns 'Did you mean ...?' suggestions in error responses for misspelled field names, enabling schema reconstruction even when introspection is disabled.
findings.impact: Attackers can use automated tools (Clairvoyance, graphql-cop) to systematically reconstruct the full schema from error-message suggestions, bypassing introspection restrictions.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable field suggestions in production. In Apollo Server: set validationRules to NoSchemaIntrospectionCustomRule and disable suggestions.

findings.title: GraphQL: GraphQL Batching Enabled Without Limit
findings.description: The GraphQL endpoint accepts batched queries (array of operations) in a single request without enforcing a batch size limit.
findings.impact: Attackers can bypass per-request rate limits by batching hundreds of queries (e.g., login mutations for credential stuffing) into a single HTTP request, evading IP-based throttling.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable batching or enforce a maximum batch size (e.g. 5). Count each batched query against the per-user rate limit.

findings.title: Authentication: GraphQL Alias-Based Rate Limit Bypass
findings.description: The GraphQL endpoint resolves multiple aliased copies of the same field in a single request, allowing attackers to multiply resolver executions and bypass per-request rate limits.
findings.impact: An attacker can send a single HTTP request with 100+ aliased resolver calls (e.g., 100 login mutations with different credentials), bypassing IP-based rate limits that count HTTP requests, not GraphQL operations.
findings.remediation_brief: Count each alias as a separate operation for rate-limiting. Implement query complexity scoring that accounts for aliases.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: OAuth Token via Endpoint
findings.description: The OAuth token info/introspection endpoint returns token metadata (scope, audience, user identity) to any bearer of the token without requiring client authentication.
findings.impact: An attacker with a leaked or stolen token can query the token info endpoint to discover the token's scope, audience, and associated user identity, enabling targeted privilege escalation.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict token info endpoints to authenticated clients only. Require client_id + client_secret for introspection requests per RFC 7662.

findings.title: Sensitive File Exposed: Postman Collection or Environment File Exposed
findings.description: Postman collection or environment files are publicly accessible. Collections expose full API endpoint inventory with example requests; environment files may contain API keys, tokens, and secrets.
findings.impact: An attacker gains a complete API endpoint map with example requests, parameters, and potentially authentication tokens from the Postman environment file, enabling targeted API attacks.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove Postman collection and environment files from public web paths. Never deploy development/testing files to production servers.

findings.title: Authentication: Rate Limit Headers Expose Throttling Configuration
findings.description: API responses include rate-limiting headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) that reveal exact throttling thresholds.
findings.impact: An attacker can read the rate limit, remaining quota, and reset window to precisely calibrate brute-force attacks to stay just under the limit, making detection harder.
findings.remediation_brief: Evaluate whether rate limit headers are necessary in production. If kept, combine with exponential backoff enforcement and account lockout.

findings.title: Web Misconfiguration: API Version Header Manipulation Yields Different Response
findings.description: The API accepts version negotiation headers (X-API-Version, Accept-Version, Api-Version) and returns different responses for different version values, indicating deprecated or beta versions may be accessible.
findings.impact: An attacker can access deprecated API versions that may have weaker security controls, missing authentication checks, or known vulnerabilities that were fixed in newer versions.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict API version negotiation. Disable access to deprecated API versions in production. Return 400 for unrecognized version headers.

findings.title: Discovery: Web Endpoint Discovered (Katana)
findings.description: Katana web crawler discovered accessible web paths, JavaScript-referenced endpoints, and linked resources on the target application. Katana performs headless or passive crawling to enumerate the full reachable surface of a web application, including dynamically generated links.
findings.impact: Discovered endpoints expand the known attack surface for further API and web security testing. Hidden or undocumented paths may expose administrative interfaces, debug endpoints, or sensitive functionality not intended for public access.
findings.remediation_brief: Review all discovered endpoints for unintended exposure. Remove or restrict access to administrative, debug, and development endpoints in production. Implement proper access controls on all discovered paths.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Forward Secrecy: Not Supported
findings.description: The API endpoint's TLS configuration does not offer forward secrecy. Cipher suites without ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE/DHE) leave all recorded API traffic vulnerable to retrospective decryption if the server's private key is later compromised.
findings.impact: API communications often carry authentication tokens, session data, and sensitive business payloads. Without forward secrecy, an attacker who captures encrypted API traffic and later obtains the private key can decrypt every recorded session retroactively.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the API server to use only cipher suites that provide forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Disable static RSA key exchange. TLSv1.3 mandates forward secrecy and should be preferred.

findings.title: AI/ML API Service Detected: {service_name}
findings.description: Active probing of common AI/ML API paths detected a responding AI service. This includes OpenAI-compatible APIs (/v1/chat/completions), Ollama (/api/generate), Gradio (/queue/join), MLflow (/api/2.0/mlflow/), Triton Inference Server (/v2/models), Streamlit (/_stcore/), and LangFlow (/api/v1/prediction). The service responded with HTTP 200, 401, 403, or 405, confirming the endpoint exists.
findings.impact: AI/ML APIs are vulnerable to prompt injection, training data extraction, model theft, output manipulation, and denial of service via resource-intensive inference requests. APIs responding with 401/403 confirm existence and may be vulnerable to authentication bypass. Unprotected AI APIs allow arbitrary model interaction without rate limiting or input validation.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict AI/ML API access to authorized clients. Implement authentication, rate limiting, and input validation on all AI endpoints. Deploy prompt injection defenses and content safety guardrails. Conduct specialized AI security testing with pAIn.

findings.title: AI/ML API Endpoints in Specification
aliases: ML Inference Endpoints in API Spec
findings.description: Analysis of the API specification (OpenAPI/Swagger/Postman/HAR) revealed endpoints with AI/ML characteristics: LLM inference paths, embedding generation, model prediction, or body fields matching known AI API schemas (prompt, messages, model, temperature, max_tokens). These spec-documented AI endpoints warrant specialized security testing beyond standard API fuzzing.
findings.impact: Documented AI endpoints may accept arbitrary prompts, return sensitive training data, or expose model internals. Standard API fuzzing typically misses AI-specific vulnerabilities like prompt injection, jailbreaking, and indirect prompt injection via RAG poisoning. The specification reveals the full AI API surface area including request schemas that can be used to craft targeted attacks.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement AI-specific input validation and output filtering on all AI/ML endpoints documented in the specification. Deploy prompt injection defenses, rate limiting, and content safety guardrails. Test with pAIn for LLM-specific vulnerabilities.
